desc:
In prefix (Polish) notation an operator is written before its two operands. The string expr consists of single digits 0-9 and the binary operators +, - and *, with no spaces and no brackets. For example +*34-82 means (3 * 4) + (8 - 2) = 18 and -92 means 9 - 2 = 7.

The string is always a valid prefix expression. Evaluate it and return the result. Note that - subtracts the second operand from the first: -29 is -7.
constraints: expr contains only the characters 0-9, '+', '-' and '*' and is a valid prefix expression
Every intermediate value fits in a signed 32-bit integer
hints: The operands of an operator come right after it. If you read the string from the right, what do you know when you reach an operator?
Scan from right to left with a stack. A digit is pushed. When you see an operator, the two operands have already been evaluated and are on the stack.
On an operator pop a first (it is the left operand, because it was pushed last) and then b, and push a op b. The answer is the single value left at the end.
editorial: Reading a prefix expression from right to left turns it into a postfix evaluation. When the scan reaches an operator, everything to its right has already been processed, so both of its operands are finished values on the stack.
Digit: push it. Operator: pop a (the top, which is the first operand because the scan runs right to left), pop b, push a op b. Getting this order wrong only matters for -, so test -29.
Time O(n), stack O(n). A recursive parser that reads left to right works as well, but with 10,000 characters its recursion could get deep, so the explicit stack is the safer choice.
